questions.question: A first-year student is asked what the field of operations research (OR) does. Which description is accurate?
options: It collects and summarizes data on past operations without recommending any decision.
It uses mathematical models and methods to support optimal or good decisions.
It replaces managers by computer rules that fix every decision automatically.
It runs day-to-day operations such as machine repairs, deliveries and stock counts.

questions.question: In an OR decision problem with an objective, available choices and restrictions on those choices, what is the role of the objective?
options: It describes which of the available choices are allowed.
It is the decision that the analysis recommends.
It is the given data the planner cannot change.
It is the criterion that ranks the allowed choices.

questions.question: OR distinguishes exact solution methods, which find a proven optimum, from heuristics, which aim for a good decision without that guarantee. When is a heuristic the appropriate choice?
options: When the problem is too hard to solve exactly in the time available.
When the problem is small, since exact methods are meant for large ones.
When the exact optimum is known but too expensive to implement.
When the data are uncertain, since a heuristic removes that uncertainty.

questions.question: Two analysts model the same staff-planning problem and both solve their models exactly, yet they recommend different rosters. What is the most likely explanation?
options: One of the exact solution methods must have made a calculation error.
OR problems never have a single answer, so any roster is acceptable.
Their models make different assumptions or use different data.
The models use different symbols, and notation changes the optimum.

questions.question: OR turns a practical planning question into a mathematical model with an objective, choices and restrictions. What does this formulation make possible?
options: Guaranteeing that the chosen plan works out in practice.
Settling which objective the planner ought to pursue.
Removing every simplification, so the model equals the situation.
Comparing all allowed choices systematically by one criterion.

questions.question: A dairy plans its weekly milk deliveries with OR. It decides how much each depot ships to each shop, wants the total transport cost to be as low as possible, and must deliver at least 500 crates to its largest shop. What is the requirement of at least 500 crates in this decision problem?
options: The objective of the dairy's problem
A restriction on the shipment choices
One of the dairy's available choices
The optimal solution of the problem

questions.question: A shop chooses one carrier for an order. Carrier A costs 120 euros and delivers in 5 days, B costs 100 and takes 8 days, C costs 140 and takes 3 days, D costs 110 and takes 6 days. The goods must arrive within 6 days, and the cost should be as low as possible. Which carrier is best?
options: Carrier B
Carrier C
Carrier D
Carrier A

questions.question: A courier can take route R1 (30 km, 50 minutes), R2 (36 km, 38 minutes) or R3 (42 km, 35 minutes). The driver wants the shortest driving time; the accountant wants the shortest distance. Which statement about the best route is correct?
options: R3 is best for time and R1 for distance.
R2 is best, as a compromise of both goals.
R1 is best for both, as shorter is faster.
No route is best until both goals are met.

questions.question: An OR model gives an optimal delivery plan, but the check against practice shows that the plan ignores the drivers' legal break times, so it cannot be carried out. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Carry out the plan, since it is optimal for the model.
Shift some deliveries by hand and keep the model as it is.
Use a heuristic instead, since the exact method has failed.
Add the break-time rules to the model and solve it again.

questions.question: A bakery's OR model decides how many loaves to bake. An analyst proposes to treat the market price of flour as one of the available choices, alongside the number of loaves. Why is this inappropriate?
options: Prices are given data, so they may not appear in the model at all.
The bakery cannot set the price; the model could pick an unreal one.
The price should be the only choice, since the loaves follow from it.
Costs belong to the objective, and objective terms cannot be chosen.

questions.question: A budget of 10 must fund projects A (cost 6, value 9), B (cost 5, value 7) and C (cost 5, value 6); the total value should be as large as possible. A quick rule takes the most valuable project first, then any that still fit. What is the best total value, and how does the rule compare?
options: 9 with A alone; taking the most valuable first is exact
16 with A and B; using 11 of the budget is close enough
22 with all three; the budget limits each project singly
13 with B and C; the rule's 9 is feasible, not optimal

questions.question: A van leaves the depot, visits 20 customers once each in some order, and returns. Its planner considers listing every visiting order and picking the shortest. How many visiting orders are there, and what does this suggest?
options: $20^2=400$; few enough to list and compare every single order
$2^{20}\approx1.0\times10^{6}$; one order for each subset of customers
$20!\approx2.4\times10^{18}$; far too many, so a heuristic may be needed
$190$; one order for each pair of neighbouring customers

questions.question: An OR model of a production decision has been solved by an exact method, which returns a proven optimal solution of the model. Which conclusion is justified without further checking?
options: No allowed choice in the model does better on its objective.
No better decision exists anywhere in the real situation.
The cost predicted by the model will be realized in practice.
Every real restriction on production is automatically met.

questions.question: Analyst A builds a detailed model of a routing problem that includes all essential limits and finds a good plan with a heuristic. Analyst B drops an essential limit to make the model easy and solves it exactly. Which assessment is justified?
options: B's plan is always better, because it is a proven optimum.
A's plan is of no use, because it is not proven to be optimal.
Both are equally useful, since both come from mathematical models.
B's optimum may be unusable, so A's plan may well be more useful.

questions.question: A workshop model chooses one of four weekly plans, making profit as large as possible with at most 40 machine hours: A (profit 300, 38 machine h, 34 labour h), B (280, 42, 26), C (260, 36, 28), D (220, 30, 20). Validation shows that only 30 labour hours exist, which the model omitted. Which plan should now be recommended?
options: Plan A
Plan C
Plan B
Plan D

questions.question: A buyer chooses one supplier: P (price 500, delivery 10 days), Q (560, 6 days), R (600, 3 days) or S (640, 2 days). Each day of waiting costs 20, and the objective is to make price plus waiting cost as low as possible. Which supplier is best?
options: Supplier P
Supplier S
Supplier R
Supplier Q

questions.question: In an OR decision problem the objective is a cost to be made as low as possible. An extra restriction is added, so fewer choices are allowed; a cheapest allowed choice exists both before and after. What happens to the best achievable cost?
options: It stays the same or becomes higher, never lower.
It becomes lower, because the model is more realistic.
It stays the same, because restrictions do not affect the objective.
It can move either way, depending on the data.
